Scraping 16,000 Jobs: ETL vs ELT and Lessons Learnt, Finale

Oct 02, 2026 · 5 MIN READ · · BRANDON T. BANDE

  • developers
  • zimbabwe

Hi,

I'm Brandon.

In Part 1 and Part 2, I went on about the thought process and the hands-on application of the concepts I ended up adopting. To wrap up the series, I will talk less about the hands-on tech stuff and reflect on the lessons learnt.

The basics matter

In two cases, my work would have been easier if I had known the basics. To be specific:

  1. The approach of just getting the data, extracting the info and then tabulating it is not as simple as A, B, C.
  2. If I had known the different ways of scraping data, I wouldn't have spent a few days learning Selenium and how to extract from WordPress.

I have always prided myself on being self-taught. At some point, I coined the term short-cut developer to describe myself. I am proud that, with no academic or guided foundation, I got on the internet and taught myself to code. But I am also aware of my limitations: things should not just work. They should work effectively, efficiently, accurately and a bunch of other important words if a system is to serve its purpose. (Funny, coming from the guy who over-engineers everything.) Back to the story.

ETL vs ELT

Extract. Transform. Load.

I had heard the abbreviations before. I had a rough idea, but I didn't know where they applied. I guess book smart is not really street smart. In my flow, it was something like this:

  • Getting the page content about a job from the internet (~5 seconds)
  • Extracting the actual fields needed using an LLM on my machine (2–6 minutes, totally offline)
  • Writing to my local database (~1 second)

So initially, I would get what I wanted after a few minutes. That worked!!! Now imagine this at scale. Cycling through 16,000 jobs would take about 533 to 1,600 hours of continuous compute. That is at least 22 days straight. The process where I obtained the page, extracted the info (transformed it) and only then loaded it for my colleague is ETL.

The cure to my pain

Hidden in plain sight was a principle that applies when you have exactly this problem. I could just store as many jobs as possible on my personal computer and then do the transformation in my own time. That is what ELT does. In my case, it was the best approach because:

  1. If my internet went down, work could still go on.
  2. I could provide up-to-date data to my colleague at regular intervals.

To top it off, I could run a few things at the same time. To achieve that, I ended up indexing all the pages that had job listings. Then, following that index, I could load page by page into my local dump of raw job text. At times, using concepts like threading, I was able to speed that up. Meanwhile, the transformation would be taking place in the background.

Another thing that came to mind: if, in the future, I realised I had missed something key, I could still go back to the raw dump and transform it again. (I did exactly that, and interestingly, I could expand on the already loaded data.)

Disclaimer

One might argue that what I did is still ETL. Technically, depending on where you draw the boundaries between extraction and transformation, they could be right. But the important difference for me was what happened after I received the data.

Instead of transforming every job immediately, I extracted the raw content, loaded it locally and transformed it later.

Extract. Load. Transform. ELT.

A bit about scraping

In the first article, I talked about the different approaches I adopted through trial and error. The key takeaway was different strokes for different folks, I guess. Another thing I should address is whether this was done the right way. There is a lot of grey area when it comes to scraping content in the public domain. I did this as educational research, and the data is not for commercial use. I also practised respectful scraping to avoid flooding the sources with requests. And I am open to discussing methods of respectful scraping that I can adopt in the future.

Writing this series is not merely about documenting my "genius moments", but about sharing the realisation that being a short-cut developer has its limits. Building something real exposes your shortfalls, and at times eating your shoe, admitting and acknowledging your limits, is the only way to grow. Looking back, the dots connect. And aha, I now know where ETL fits and where it doesn't. 18,693 job posts say so :)

Finale. Curtains close.
